Revenue: NVIDIA reported $60.92 billion in fiscal 2024 [DB].
The boost came from strong demand for AI inference platforms, generative-AI workloads, and cloud-provider adoption [3][2].
Gaming growth: Gaming revenue rose 15% to $10.4 billion, helped by higher sell-in to partners as inventory levels normalized [3][2].
Overall mix: The combined growth of Compute & Networking (Data Center) and Graphics (Gaming) segments lifted total revenue 126% from the prior year [2][6].
Management commentary: NVIDIA’s MD&A notes that the revenue increase was “up 126% from a year ago” and attributes it primarily to the explosive Data Center demand driven by AI applications [2].
Answer: Tesla’s revenue grew 51.4 % in fiscal 2022 [DB].
Overall revenue rise: Total revenues reached $81.46 billion, up $27.64 billion from 2021, reflecting higher vehicle deliveries, new production capacity, and expanded operations [4].

Automotive sales: $67.21 billion in automotive sales, a $23.09 billion (52 %) jump, driven by 347,024 more Model 3/Y deliveries and 38,183 more Model S/X deliveries, plus higher average selling prices from production ramps at Gigafactory Shanghai, Texas, and Berlin [5].
Services & other: $6.09 billion, up $2.29 billion (60 %), from growth in used-vehicle sales, non-warranty maintenance, paid Supercharging, insurance, and retail merchandise [2].
Automotive leasing: $2.48 billion, up $834 million (51 %), due to a larger lease portfolio and more direct-sales-type leasing activity [2][8].
Energy generation & storage: $3.91 billion, up $1.12 billion (40 %), helped by higher Megapack and Powerwall deployments and higher solar system prices [2][6].
Regulatory credits: $1.78 billion, up $311 million (21 %), from additional credit consideration in Q1 2022 [2].

Loss on sale of a subsidiary: The consolidated statement of operations shows an $8.31 billion loss on the sale of a subsidiary and subsidiaries held for sale in 2024, a line item that did not appear in 2023 [2].

Lower earnings before taxes: Earnings before income taxes fell to $20.07 billion in 2024 from $29.11 billion in 2023, reflecting weaker operating performance (revenues rose but operating costs grew faster) [2].

Tax provision impact: Although the provision for income taxes decreased, it was not enough to offset the large one-time loss, resulting in a net income drop of $7.98 billion (-35.6 %) year-over-year [DB].

Net income: Nucor reported net income of $6.83 billion for fiscal 2021[DB].

Record-high profitability across all segments – the steel-mills segment ran at a 94 % average utilization rate, with volume growth and average selling-price increases that outpaced raw-material cost hikes[5].
Strong demand in steel products – non-residential construction demand boosted the steel-products segment, delivering its most profitable year ever[5].
Overall segment strength – both the steel-mills and steel-products units posted very strong margins, contributing to the “most profitable year in the Company’s history”[5].
These operational drivers translated into a net-income margin of 18.7 % of net sales[6], up from 3.6 % in 2020.

Higher non-interest revenue (NIR): NIR increased 11% to $68.8 billion, also boosted by the First Republic acquisition (including a $2.8 billion bargain-purchase gain) and higher asset-management fees[1].
Airbnb’s net income in fiscal 2023 was $4.79 billion[DB], compared with $1.89 billion in fiscal 2022[DB].
Revenue growth – an 18 % increase to $9.9 billion, boosting overall profitability[1].
Higher interest income – interest income jumped from $186 million to $721 million (a 288 % rise) as cash balances grew and rates rose[8].
Cost-structure discipline – management cited continued control of operating expenses[1].
Tax benefit – a portion of a $2.9 billion valuation allowance on deferred tax assets was released, reducing tax expense[1].
These factors together produced the sharp increase in net income and the jump in net margin from 22.5 % in 2022 to 48.3 % in 2023[DB].
Answer: AT&T reported a net loss of $8.52 billion in fiscal 2022[DB].
Operating loss: Operating income was a loss of $4.587 billion[4], reflecting weaker service revenues after the 2021 separation of the U.S. video business and other divestitures[8].
Asset impairments: The company recorded $27.5 billion of asset impairments and restructuring charges, a major drag on earnings[8].
Interest expense: Net interest expense of $6.108 billion added further pressure[4].
Other factors: Lower wireline demand, reduced Business Wireline revenues, and the impact of the video-business separation contributed to the revenue decline and overall loss[8].
